newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH LEADERS PUSH CABINET CHANGE TALKS TO FRIDAY.
newsitem.headline: CZECH LEADERS PUSH CABINET CHANGE TALKS TO FRIDAY.

text.p: Leaders of the three parties in the Czech ruling coalition failed to complete an agreement on changes to the cabinet on Thursday, but scheduled a breakfast meeting for Friday to continue the talks, party officials said.

President Vaclav Havel, after meeting Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and leaders of the two junior parties in the centre-right coalition said he thought Wednesday's coalition agreement to change seats in the beleaguered cabinet was proper.

"With satisfaction I recei ved information that.. representatives of this coalition have the willingness to cooperate... to govern further in this country," Havel told a news conference after the meeting.
Havel suggested that some ministerial seats might be taken by experts not affiliated with any of the three parties.
"In my opinion it is thinkable that one or another post would be taken by an expert enjoying the confidence the coalition parties, but not coming from their ranks."
An opposition resolution in parliament on Thursday calling on Havel to recall the cabinet failed to gather support.

Klaus, who leads the senior Civic Democratic Party (ODS), agreed with his coalition partners on Wednesday that a change was needed amid slumping approval ratings and an economic downturn which has sapped confidence in the government.

The cabinet shuffle has become even more sensitive as pressure mounts on the Czech crown which has been battered by foreign speculators reacting to poor macroeconomic results and political instability.

The crown earlier on Thursday fell to a record low of six percent below parity with the central bank's mark/dollar peg, and some Czechs begain asking if they should start converting their crowns into major currencies.
When Havel was asked if he would change any of the substantial wealth he has earned into a foreign currency, the president said laconically:

"You are probably refering to my millions... I will of course deposit them on a crown account, not at a foreign exchange one. I would condsider that gratuitous and totally ridiculous to change my money into dollars."
"The political situation is a little tense but it happens in a democracy from time to time," Havel added.

While speculation on which ministers might lose their seat in the cabinet focused primarily on Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik and Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy, no concrete proposals have been revealed by the party leaders.

Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec told commercial TV Nova on Thursday that a reported plan for him to replace Kocarnik as finance minister with the former ambassador to Washington Michael Zantovsky taking over as foreign minister was "not on the table, so I won't discuss it."
